items.prompt:
Choose the correct option to fill the blank.

The list of successful candidates ______ been put up on the notice board.

steps: The subject is 'list' (singular); 'of successful candidates' only describes it. So the verb is 'has been put up'.
Completed sentence: *The list of successful candidates has been put up on the notice board.*
solution.trap: 'candidates' is closest to the blank and pulls you towards 'have'.
solution.rule: The verb agrees with the head noun, not with the noun inside an 'of' phrase

items.prompt:
Choose the correct option to fill the blank.

She waited for ______ hour at the bus stop before the bus finally came.

steps: 'hour' begins with a silent 'h', so it starts with a vowel sound and takes 'an'. 'few', 'many' and 'much' cannot go before a singular countable noun.
Completed sentence: *She waited for an hour at the bus stop before the bus finally came.*
solution.trap: The letter 'h' looks like a consonant, but the article follows the sound.
solution.rule: Articles: 'an' before a vowel sound (an hour, an honest man)

items.prompt:
Choose the correct option to fill the blank.

The meeting will begin ______ 10 a.m. sharp.

steps: An exact clock time takes 'at' (at 10 a.m.); 'on' is for days and dates, 'in' for months, years and parts of the day.
Completed sentence: *The meeting will begin at 10 a.m. sharp.*
solution.trap: 'since' needs a perfect tense and a starting point; it cannot follow 'will begin'.
solution.rule: Prepositions of time: at + clock time, on + day/date, in + month/year

items.prompt:
Choose the correct option to fill the blank.

Look! The children ______ in the rain.

steps: 'Look!' shows that the action is happening right now, so the present continuous 'are playing' is needed.
Completed sentence: *Look! The children are playing in the rain.*
solution.trap: 'play' is the simple present, used for habits, not for something happening now.
solution.rule: Present continuous for an action happening at the moment of speaking

items.prompt:
Choose the correct option to fill the blank.

Between you and ______, the plan is unlikely to work.

steps: 'Between' is a preposition, and a pronoun after a preposition takes the object form: 'between you and me'.
Completed sentence: *Between you and me, the plan is unlikely to work.*
solution.trap: 'between you and I' sounds polite but is an error.
solution.rule: Pronouns: object form after a preposition

items.prompt:
Choose the correct option to fill the blank.

Of all the students in the class, Ravi is the ______.

steps: 'Of all the students' compares Ravi with more than two people, so the superlative 'tallest' is needed.
Completed sentence: *Of all the students in the class, Ravi is the tallest.*
solution.trap: 'most tallest' is a double superlative; 'tall' already takes -est.
solution.rule: Superlative for comparing one with three or more

items.prompt:
Choose the correct option to fill the blank.

My grandmother enjoys ______ old Hindi songs on the radio.

steps: 'enjoy' is always followed by a gerund (-ing form): 'enjoys listening to'.
Completed sentence: *My grandmother enjoys listening to old Hindi songs on the radio.*
solution.trap: 'enjoys to listen' is a common error; 'enjoy' never takes a to-infinitive.
solution.rule: Gerund after verbs like enjoy, avoid, finish, mind

items.prompt:
Choose the correct option to fill the blank.

She can speak Tamil, ______?

steps: A positive statement takes a negative tag, and the tag repeats the helping verb 'can': 'can't she?'.
Completed sentence: *She can speak Tamil, can't she?*
solution.trap: 'doesn't she' would need a sentence without a helping verb, like 'She speaks Tamil'.
solution.rule: Question tags: positive statement → negative tag with the same helping verb

items.prompt:
Choose the correct option to fill the blank.

One of my friends ______ a new bicycle.

steps: The subject is 'One' (of my friends), which is singular, so the verb is singular: 'has bought'.
Completed sentence: *One of my friends has bought a new bicycle.*
solution.trap: 'friends' is next to the verb, but it is not the subject.
solution.rule: 'One of the + plural noun' takes a singular verb

items.prompt: Which of the following sentences is grammatically correct?
options: Each of the boys has brought his lunch.
Each of the boys have brought their lunch.
Neither of the girls were ready for the test.
Every student and teacher were present.
The box of apples are on the table.

steps: 'Each of the boys has' is correct: 'each' is singular.
The others need 'has', 'was', 'was' and 'is': 'neither of', 'every … and every …' and 'The box' are all singular subjects.
solution.trap: A plural noun after 'of' does not make the subject plural.
solution.rule: Each, every, either, neither → singular verb

items.prompt: Which of the following sentences is grammatically incorrect? If all the sentences are correct, choose 'All are correct'.
options: If you heat water to 100 degrees Celsius, it boils.
If I see her, I will give her the message.
If it will rain tomorrow, we will stay at home.
If he had studied, he would have passed.

steps: 'If it will rain' is wrong: in a first conditional the 'if' clause takes the simple present: 'If it rains tomorrow, we will stay at home'.
The other three are correct zero, first and third conditionals.
solution.trap: 'tomorrow' tempts you to put 'will' in both clauses.
solution.rule: First conditional: If + simple present, will + verb

items.prompt:
Choose the correct option to fill the blank.

She sings very ______.

steps: The blank describes how she sings (the verb), so an adverb is needed: 'sweetly'.
Completed sentence: *She sings very sweetly.*
solution.trap: 'sweet' is an adjective; it describes a noun (a sweet voice), not a verb.
solution.rule: An adverb, not an adjective, describes an action verb

items.prompt:
Choose the correct option to fill the blank.

I ______ in this city since 2015.

steps: 'since 2015' marks an action that began in the past and is still going on, so the present perfect 'have lived' is needed.
Completed sentence: *I have lived in this city since 2015.*
solution.trap: 'am living since 2015' is a common Indian-English error.
solution.rule: Present perfect with 'since' / 'for' for an action continuing to the present

items.prompt:
Choose the correct option to fill the blank.

He is ______ European who has settled in Goa.

steps: 'European' begins with a 'yoo' sound, which is a consonant sound, so the article is 'a'.
Completed sentence: *He is a European who has settled in Goa.*
solution.trap: 'European' starts with the vowel letter 'E', but the sound is 'yoo'.
solution.rule: Articles: 'a' before a consonant sound (a European, a university, a one-rupee coin)

items.prompt: Which of the following sentences is grammatically correct?
options: The farmer died of cholera last year.
They discussed about the plan for hours.
We reached at the station late.

steps: 'die of' a disease is correct.
The others should be 'fond of music', 'prefers tea to coffee', 'discussed the plan' (no preposition) and 'reached the station' (no preposition).
solution.trap: 'discuss about' and 'reach at' add a preposition where none is needed.
solution.rule: Prepositions: fixed pairs (die of, fond of, prefer … to) and verbs that take no preposition (discuss, reach)

items.prompt: Which of the following sentences is grammatically incorrect? If all the sentences are correct, choose 'All are correct'.
options: Let you and I finish the work first.
The book is hers, not yours.
They blamed themselves for the delay.

steps: 'Let' is followed by the object form, so it should be 'Let you and me finish the work first'.
The other sentences use the pronouns correctly: 'She and I' as subject, 'hers' and 'yours' as possessives, 'themselves' as a reflexive.
solution.trap: Remove 'you and': 'Let I finish' is clearly wrong.
solution.rule: Pronouns: object form after 'let' and after prepositions

items.prompt: Which of the following sentences is grammatically correct?
options: While walking to the office, a stray dog began following me.
Having finished the work, the lights were switched off.
Driving through the ghat, the valley looked beautiful.
While I was walking to the office, a stray dog began following me.
After eating lunch, the bus left for Ooty.

steps: Only the correct sentence has a full clause ('I was walking') with its own subject.
In the others the opening phrase attaches to the wrong subject: the dog was not walking to the office, the lights did not finish the work, the valley was not driving, and the bus did not eat lunch.
solution.trap: The first wrong option is almost identical to the right one; only the missing 'I was' separates them.
solution.rule: A participle phrase at the start must refer to the subject of the main clause

items.prompt:
Choose the correct option to fill the blank.

If I ______ you, I would apologise at once.

steps: An imaginary present situation ('If I … you') takes the second conditional: If + past (were for all persons), would + verb.
Completed sentence: *If I were you, I would apologise at once.*
solution.trap: 'had been' would need 'would have apologised'.
solution.rule: Second conditional: If + past (were), would + verb

items.prompt: Which of the following sentences is grammatically correct?
options: She likes reading, to write and painting.
He is honest, hard-working and has intelligence.
The job requires patience, skill and to be honest.
We went there to relax, to eat and for shopping.
She likes reading, writing and painting.

steps: All three items in the correct sentence are gerunds.
The others mix forms: gerunds with an infinitive, adjectives with a verb phrase, nouns with an infinitive, and infinitives with a prepositional phrase.
solution.trap: Each wrong sentence breaks the pattern only in its last item.
solution.rule: Parallelism: items joined by 'and' must have the same grammatical form

items.prompt:
Choose the correct option to fill the blank.

Nobody came to the party, ______?

steps: 'Nobody' makes the statement negative, so the tag is positive. Indefinite pronouns like 'nobody' are referred to by 'they': 'did they?'.
Completed sentence: *Nobody came to the party, did they?*
solution.trap: 'Nobody came' has no 'not', so it looks positive.
solution.rule: Question tags: negative words (nobody, never, hardly) take a positive tag; nobody / everybody → they

items.prompt:
Choose the correct option to fill the blank.

He is used to ______ late at night.

steps: In 'be used to' the word 'to' is a preposition, so it is followed by a gerund: 'is used to working'.
Completed sentence: *He is used to working late at night.*
solution.trap: Do not confuse it with 'used to work' (a past habit).
solution.rule: be used to / look forward to / object to + -ing

items.prompt: Which of the following sentences is grammatically incorrect? If all the sentences are correct, choose 'All are correct'.
options: He is more stronger than his brother.
This is the best film I have seen this year.
Mumbai is larger than any other city in Maharashtra.
She is senior to me by two years.

steps: 'more stronger' is a double comparative; it should be 'stronger'.
The other three are correct: a superlative, 'any other' within the same group, and 'senior to'.
solution.trap: 'senior to' looks odd but is correct; Latin comparatives take 'to'.
solution.rule: Do not use 'more' with a comparative already ending in -er

items.prompt:
Choose the correct option to fill the blank.

Neither the manager nor his assistants ______ available on Saturday.

steps: With 'neither … nor' the verb agrees with the nearer subject, 'assistants' (plural), so the plural 'were' is the only correct form offered.
Completed sentence: *Neither the manager nor his assistants were available on Saturday.*
solution.trap: 'Neither' alone takes a singular verb, but 'neither … nor' follows the nearer noun.
solution.rule: Neither … nor / either … or: the verb agrees with the nearer subject

items.prompt:
Choose the correct option to fill the blank.

One of the lights in the corridor ______ out of order since Monday.

steps: The subject is 'One' (singular), and 'since Monday' needs the present perfect: 'has been out of order'.
Completed sentence: *One of the lights in the corridor has been out of order since Monday.*
solution.trap: 'have been' agrees with 'lights', which is not the subject.
solution.rule: 'One of the + plural noun' takes a singular verb; 'since' needs a perfect tense

items.prompt: Which of the following sentences is grammatically correct?
options: By the time we reached the cinema, the film had started.
He did not came to the office yesterday.

steps: The correct sentence uses the past perfect for the earlier of two past actions.
The others should be 'I saw him yesterday', 'She knows the answer' (know is not used in the continuous), 'did not come', and 'have been living here since 2010'.
solution.trap: 'did not came' uses two past forms; after 'did' the base verb is used.
solution.rule: Tenses: past perfect for the earlier past action; no present perfect with a finished time

items.prompt:
Choose the correct option to fill the blank.

______ Ganga is considered a sacred river by millions of people.

steps: Names of rivers take the definite article: 'The Ganga', 'the Narmada'.
Completed sentence: *The Ganga is considered a sacred river by millions of people.*
solution.trap: Most proper names take no article, but rivers are an exception.
solution.rule: Articles: 'the' before names of rivers, seas, oceans and mountain ranges

items.prompt: Which of the following sentences is grammatically incorrect? If all the sentences are correct, choose 'All are correct'.
options: He drives carefully on the highway.
She looks beautifully in that saree.

steps: 'look' here is a linking verb (it describes her appearance), so it takes an adjective: 'She looks beautiful'.
'tastes delicious' is also a linking verb with an adjective; 'drives carefully' and 'running late' are correct.
solution.trap: 'beautifully' sounds more formal, but linking verbs do not take adverbs.
solution.rule: Linking verbs (look, seem, taste, feel, smell) take adjectives

items.prompt:
Choose the correct option to fill the blank.

The new rule will come ______ effect from 1 April.

steps: The fixed phrase is 'come into effect' (or 'come into force').
Completed sentence: *The new rule will come into effect from 1 April.*
solution.trap: 'come in effect' is a frequent slip.
solution.rule: Fixed phrase: come into effect / force

items.prompt: Which of the following sentences is grammatically correct?
options: He hardly ever comes late, doesn't he?
They are going to Agra, isn't it?
There is a bank nearby, isn't it?
Let's go for a walk, shall we?

steps: After 'Let's' (a suggestion) the tag is 'shall we?'.
The others should be 'does he?' (hardly is negative), 'aren't they?', 'isn't there?' and 'can she?'.
solution.trap: 'isn't it?' is the all-purpose tag of spoken Indian English, but it is not correct in writing.
solution.rule: Question tags repeat the helping verb and the subject pronoun, with the opposite polarity

items.prompt:
Choose the correct option to fill the blank.

Had I known about the sale, I ______ more books.

steps: 'Had I known' is an inverted third conditional (= If I had known), so the result is 'would have bought'.
Completed sentence: *Had I known about the sale, I would have bought more books.*
solution.trap: The missing 'if' hides that this is a conditional.
solution.rule: Third conditional: If + had + past participle, would have + past participle

items.prompt: Which of the following sentences is grammatically incorrect? If all the sentences are correct, choose 'All are correct'.
options: The quality of the mangoes were not good.
Bread and butter is a common breakfast.
The jury has given its verdict.
Ten kilometres is a long distance to walk.

steps: The subject is 'quality' (singular), so it should be 'was not good'.
The others are correct: 'bread and butter' is one dish, the jury acts as one body, and a distance is one amount.
solution.trap: 'Bread and butter is' looks wrong but is correct.
solution.rule: The verb agrees with the head noun, not the noun in the 'of' phrase

items.prompt:
Choose the correct option to fill the blank.

The committee has submitted ______ report to the board.

steps: 'The committee has' treats the committee as a single body, so the possessive is 'its'.
Completed sentence: *The committee has submitted its report to the board.*
solution.trap: 'it's' looks possessive because of the apostrophe.
solution.rule: Pronouns: 'its' is the possessive; 'it's' means 'it is'

items.prompt:
Choose the correct option to fill the blank.

She is one of those officers who ______ never late for work.

steps: 'who' refers to 'officers' (plural), not to 'one', so the verb in the relative clause is plural: 'who are never late'.
Completed sentence: *She is one of those officers who are never late for work.*
solution.trap: The singular rule for 'one of the …' applies to the main verb, not to the 'who' clause.
solution.rule: In 'one of those + plural noun + who …', the relative clause takes a plural verb

items.prompt: Which of the following sentences is grammatically correct?
options: Not only the students but also the teacher were surprised.
A pair of shoes were lying under the bed.
The number of accidents have gone down.
The captain, along with his players, was received at the airport.
Either you or he are responsible.

steps: 'along with his players' does not change the subject 'The captain', so 'was' is right.
The others need 'was' (the nearer subject 'teacher'), 'was' ('A pair'), 'has' ('The number') and 'is' (the nearer subject 'he').
solution.trap: 'the teacher were' fails because the verb follows the nearer subject in 'not only … but also'.
solution.rule: 'along with', 'as well as', 'together with' do not change the number of the subject

items.prompt:
Choose the correct option to fill the blank.

I ______ for two hours when the power finally came back.

steps: A continuing action with a duration ('for two hours') that ended at a past moment ('came back') takes the past perfect continuous.
Completed sentence: *I had been waiting for two hours when the power finally came back.*
solution.trap: 'have been waiting' measures up to now, but 'came back' fixes the time in the past.
solution.rule: Past perfect continuous: duration up to a point in the past

items.prompt: Which of the following sentences is grammatically incorrect? If all the sentences are correct, choose 'All are correct'.
options: The gold in this ring is of poor quality.
The gold is a precious metal.
He goes to church every Sunday.
The rich should help the poor.

steps: A material in general takes no article: 'Gold is a precious metal'.
'The gold in this ring' is correct because it is specific; 'go to church' (for worship) and 'the rich' (a class of people) are correct.
solution.trap: The first correct sentence also has 'The gold', but there it refers to particular gold.
solution.rule: Articles: no article for materials and abstract nouns used in a general sense

items.prompt:
Choose the correct option to fill the blank.

The climate of Bengaluru is milder than ______ of Chennai.

steps: The comparison must be between climate and climate, so a singular pronoun standing for 'the climate' is needed: 'that of Chennai'.
Completed sentence: *The climate of Bengaluru is milder than that of Chennai.*
solution.trap: 'those' is plural and cannot replace 'climate'.
solution.rule: Compare like with like: 'that of' (singular), 'those of' (plural)

items.prompt: Which of the following sentences is grammatically correct?
options: She avoided to meet him at the function.
They look forward to meet you.
I remember locking the door before I left.
He is capable to handle the pressure.
We are considering to shift to Pune.

steps: 'remember + -ing' refers to a memory of an earlier action, which fits 'before I left'.
The others need 'avoided meeting', 'look forward to meeting', 'capable of handling' and 'considering shifting'.
solution.trap: 'capable to' is a common slip; the adjective takes 'of' + -ing.
solution.rule: Gerund after avoid, consider, look forward to, capable of

items.prompt:
Choose the correct option to fill the blank.

If she had taken the job in Delhi last year, she ______ in a bigger flat now.

steps: This is a mixed conditional: an unreal past condition ('had taken … last year') with a present result ('now'), so 'would be living'.
Completed sentence: *If she had taken the job in Delhi last year, she would be living in a bigger flat now.*
solution.trap: 'would have lived' refers to the past and clashes with 'now'.
solution.rule: Mixed conditional: If + past perfect, would + verb (present result)

items.prompt: Which of the following sentences is grammatically incorrect? If all the sentences are correct, choose 'All are correct'.
options: The manager asked us to finish the report, check the figures and that we should send it by noon.
He was praised not only for his courage but also for his honesty.
She would rather walk than take the bus.
Either we leave now or we miss the train.

steps: The list after 'asked us' mixes infinitives with a 'that' clause; it should be 'to finish the report, check the figures and send it by noon'.
The other three keep matching forms after 'not only … but also', 'rather … than' and 'either … or'.
solution.trap: The error appears only in the last item of the list.
solution.rule: Parallelism: every item in a list must have the same form

items.prompt: Which of the following sentences is grammatically correct?
options: Having missed the last bus, an auto was our only option.
Being a holiday, the offices were closed.
On entering the hall, the lights went off.
Having missed the last bus, we had to take an auto.
Walking in the park, a snake frightened the children.

steps: 'we' missed the bus, so the opening phrase attaches correctly.
In the others the phrase dangles: an auto did not miss the bus, the offices were not a holiday, the lights did not enter the hall, and the snake was not walking in the park.
solution.trap: 'Being a holiday' needs 'It being a holiday' to be correct.
solution.rule: Dangling modifier: an opening phrase must describe the subject that follows it

items.prompt:
Choose the correct option to fill the blank.

I am late again, ______?

steps: The accepted negative tag for 'I am' is 'aren't I?'.
Completed sentence: *I am late again, aren't I?*
solution.trap: 'amn't I' seems logical but is not standard; 'am not I' has the wrong word order (it would be 'am I not?').
solution.rule: Question tags: 'I am …, aren't I?'

items.prompt: Which of the following sentences is grammatically incorrect? If all the sentences are correct, choose 'All are correct'.
options: He has been absent since three days.
The house was built of stone.
We congratulated her on her success.

steps: 'three days' is a length of time, so it takes 'for': 'absent for three days'.
The others are correct: good at, built of, congratulate on.
solution.trap: The present perfect makes 'since' feel right, but the noun is a duration.
solution.rule: since + point of time; for + length of time

items.prompt:
Choose the correct option to fill the blank.

The patient is doing ______ after the operation.

steps: 'doing' is an action verb, so the adverb 'well' is needed to describe how the patient is progressing.
Completed sentence: *The patient is doing well after the operation.*
solution.trap: 'doing good' is common in speech but is not correct for health.
solution.rule: 'well' is the adverb (and the adjective for health); 'good' is only an adjective

items.prompt: Which of the following sentences is grammatically correct?
options: The manager and I have been invited to the conference.
Me and my brother went to Agra.
This is between he and his wife.
Whom do you think is the best candidate?
The prize was shared by Ravi and I.

steps: 'The manager and I' is a subject, so the subject form 'I' is correct.
The others need 'My brother and I' (subject), 'between him and his wife' and 'by Ravi and me' (objects of prepositions), and 'Who … is' (subject of 'is').
solution.trap: 'Whom do you think is …' looks formal but 'who' is the subject of 'is'.
solution.rule: Subject pronouns (I, he, who) as subjects; object pronouns (me, him, whom) after verbs and prepositions

items.prompt:
Choose the correct option to fill the blank.

Twenty thousand rupees ______ too much to pay for a phone like this.

steps: A sum of money treated as one amount takes a singular verb: 'Twenty thousand rupees is too much'.
Completed sentence: *Twenty thousand rupees is too much to pay for a phone like this.*
solution.trap: The plural noun 'rupees' pulls you towards 'are'.
solution.rule: Amounts of money, time and distance taken as a whole → singular verb

items.prompt: Which of the following sentences is grammatically incorrect? If all the sentences are correct, choose 'All are correct'.
options: One of the windows is broken.
She is one of the students who have been selected for the camp.
Each one of the buses has a first-aid kit.
Neither of the answers is correct.

steps: All four sentences are correct.

'One of the windows is' and 'Each one of the buses has' take a singular verb; in 'one of the students who have been selected', 'who' refers to 'students', so the verb is plural; 'Neither of' takes a singular verb.
solution.trap: The second sentence looks like an agreement error, but it is correct.
solution.rule: 'One of the …' → singular main verb; 'one of the … who' → plural verb in the 'who' clause

items.prompt:
Choose the correct option to fill the blank.

The minister refused ______ any questions about the project.

steps: 'refuse' is followed by a to-infinitive: 'refused to answer'.
Completed sentence: *The minister refused to answer any questions about the project.*
solution.trap: 'to answering' would need a verb like 'objected to', not 'refused'.
solution.rule: to-infinitive after refuse, decide, agree, promise, hope

items.prompt: Which of the following sentences is grammatically correct?
options: Had the bank raised its rates, borrowers would feel the pinch last year.
Should the bank will raise its rates, borrowers would feel the pinch.
If the bank would raise its rates, borrowers would have felt the pinch.
Were the bank to raise its rates, borrowers would feel the pinch.
Were the bank raised its rates, borrowers would feel the pinch.

steps: 'Were the bank to raise …, borrowers would feel …' is a correct inverted hypothetical (= If the bank were to raise).
The others fail: 'last year' needs 'would have felt'; 'Should … will raise' doubles the modal; 'If … would raise' puts 'would' in the if-clause; 'Were the bank raised its rates' mixes two verbs.
solution.trap: Each wrong option looks formal; check the tense of each clause.
solution.rule: Inverted conditionals: Were + subject + to-infinitive; Should + subject + base verb; Had + subject + past participle

items.prompt: Which of the following sentences is grammatically incorrect? If all the sentences are correct, choose 'All are correct'.
options: The committee's recommendations, along with the dissenting note, has been forwarded to the ministry.
Neither the chairman nor the directors were aware of the lapse.
What the bank needs now is patient capital.
A number of branches have been merged this year.

steps: The subject is 'recommendations' (plural); 'along with the dissenting note' does not change it, so 'have been forwarded'.
The others are correct: the nearer subject 'directors' → were; a 'What' clause → is; 'A number of' → plural.
solution.trap: 'note' is next to the verb and is singular, which makes 'has' sound right.
solution.rule: Phrases with 'along with' do not change the number of the subject

items.prompt:
Choose the correct option to fill the blank.

Scarcely ______ the results when the website crashed.

steps: 'Scarcely' at the start forces inversion, and the earlier of the two past actions takes the past perfect: 'Scarcely had the board announced … when …'.
Completed sentence: *Scarcely had the board announced the results when the website crashed.*
solution.trap: 'did the board announce' inverts correctly but uses the wrong tense.
solution.rule: Scarcely / Hardly + had + subject + past participle … when + past

items.prompt: Which of the following sentences is grammatically correct?
options: The policy aims not only to curb inflation but also supporting growth.
The policy not only aims to curb inflation but also to support growth.
The policy aims at curbing inflation and to support growth.
The policy aims to curb inflation as well as supporting growth.
The policy aims not only to curb inflation but also to support growth.

steps: After 'not only' and 'but also' the same form (to-infinitive) follows, and 'not only' sits right before what it pairs.
The others mismatch forms or misplace 'not only' (it stands before 'aims' but pairs 'to curb' with 'to support').
solution.trap: The second wrong option has the right verbs but 'not only' in the wrong place.
solution.rule: Correlatives (not only … but also, either … or) must be followed by matching forms

items.prompt: Which of the following sentences is grammatically incorrect? If all the sentences are correct, choose 'All are correct'.
options: Rushing to catch the train, I let my bag slip off my shoulder.
Weather permitting, the match will begin at nine.
Rushing to catch the train, my bag slipped off my shoulder.
Considering the circumstances, the decision was reasonable.

steps: The opening phrase describes a person, but the subject is 'my bag', so the modifier dangles.
'Weather permitting' is an absolute phrase with its own subject, and 'Considering' works as a preposition here; both are correct.
solution.trap: 'Considering …' and 'Weather permitting' look like dangling phrases but are accepted fixed uses.
solution.rule: Dangling modifier: the subject of the main clause must be the doer of the opening phrase

items.prompt:
Choose the correct option to fill the blank.

Of the two proposals, the second is ______.

steps: With exactly two items the comparative is used, and 'the' is used because the comparison is 'of the two': 'the more practical'.
Completed sentence: *Of the two proposals, the second is the more practical.*
solution.trap: 'the most practical' is used only for three or more.
solution.rule: Comparative, not superlative, when comparing two; 'the' + comparative with 'of the two'

items.prompt: Which of the following sentences is grammatically correct?
options: She has a flair for languages and speaks French fluently.
The honesty is the best policy.
He is a MBA from a reputed institute.
She is best student in the class.
He was a honest officer throughout his career.

steps: 'a flair for' takes the indefinite article, and names of languages take none.
The others need 'Honesty is' (abstract noun in general), 'an MBA' (M is said 'em'), 'the best student' (superlative), and 'an honest officer' (silent h).
solution.trap: 'a MBA' looks right because M is a consonant letter, but it is said 'em'.
solution.rule: Articles: 'an' before a vowel sound (an MBA, an honest); 'the' before a superlative; none before abstract nouns in general

items.prompt:
Choose the correct option to fill the blank.

The auditor objected ______ the accounts without supporting vouchers.

steps: In 'object to', 'to' is a preposition, so a gerund follows: 'objected to passing'.
Completed sentence: *The auditor objected to passing the accounts without supporting vouchers.*
solution.trap: 'objected to pass' treats 'to' as part of an infinitive.
solution.rule: object to / be averse to / be committed to + -ing

items.prompt: Which of the following sentences is grammatically incorrect? If all the sentences are correct, choose 'All are correct'.
options: Few people knew the answer, did they?
Don't forget to lock the door, will you?
There's hardly any milk left, is there?
You'd better leave now, wouldn't you?

steps: 'You'd better' is short for 'You had better', so the tag is 'hadn't you?'.
The others are correct: 'few' and 'hardly' are negative (positive tags), and a negative imperative takes 'will you?'.
solution.trap: The contraction 'd hides 'had'; it is easy to read it as 'would'.
solution.rule: Question tags: 'd better = had better → hadn't you?

items.prompt:
Choose the correct option to fill the blank.

This is one of the few branches in the district that ______ a locker facility.

steps: 'that' refers to 'branches' (plural): several branches offer lockers, and this is one of them. So the verb is plural: 'offer'.
Completed sentence: *This is one of the few branches in the district that offer a locker facility.*
solution.trap: 'This is one' is singular, which makes 'offers' tempting.
solution.rule: In 'one of the … that / who …', the relative clause verb agrees with the plural noun

items.prompt: Which of the following sentences is grammatically correct?
options: The train arrived lately because of the fog.
The newly appointed officer spoke firmly but politely.
She sings good for a beginner.
He is a hardly worker who never takes leave.
The project was near complete when the funds ran out.

steps: 'newly' modifies the adjective 'appointed', and 'firmly' and 'politely' modify 'spoke'.
The others need 'arrived late' (lately means recently), 'sings well', 'a hard worker', and 'nearly complete'.
solution.trap: 'lately' and 'hardly' are not the adverbs of 'late' and 'hard'.
solution.rule: Adjective vs adverb: late / lately, hard / hardly, near / nearly have different meanings

items.prompt: Which of the following sentences is grammatically incorrect? If all the sentences are correct, choose 'All are correct'.
options: The loan was sanctioned in spite of his poor credit history.
She was accused of forging the signature.
The new scheme is on a par with the old one.
He has been working here for the past decade.

steps: All four sentences are correct.
'in spite of', 'accused of + -ing', 'on a par with' (equal to) and 'for the past decade' (a period with the present perfect continuous) are all standard.
solution.trap: A long, formal sentence feels as if it must hide an error, but each preposition here is the fixed, correct one.
solution.rule: Prepositions: in spite of, accused of, on a par with, for + period
